Title: Apprentice - First Year
Description:
Apprentice Electrician - First Year
What Does a First-Year Apprentice Do?
First-year apprentices learn the foundational concepts of electrical systems through hands-on experience and classroom learning. They develop essential skills such as installing electrical systems, working with conduits, and learning basic electrical safety practices. They work under the direct supervision of a journeyperson and are introduced to the fundamentals of electrical construction.
What Skills Are Required?
Basic understanding of direct current (DC) calculations, Ohm's Law, and power equations.
Familiarity with electrical energy sources like batteries.
Knowledge of nominal AC voltages (single-phase and three-phase).
Ability to identify various electrical components and understand panel board layouts.
Skill in bending and installing EMT conduits with hand benders.
Basic ability to pull wire and cable (up to #2 gauge).
Understanding of three-way and four-way switching systems​.
Recommended Credentials
Customer Experience Level 1
Jobsite Safety Level 1
Personal Safety Level 1
Installation Level 1
Lockout/Tagout​.

Title: Apprentice - Fourth Year
Description:
Apprentice Electrician - Fourth Year
What Does a Fourth-Year Apprentice Do?
By the fourth year, apprentices are highly skilled and nearing journeyperson-level proficiency. They can work on complex systems, including motor controls, hazardous installations, and uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems. They also acquire advanced knowledge in electrical theory, system design, and installation safety.
What Skills Are Required?
Advanced motor control and instrument hook-ups.
Installation and maintenance of UPS systems and components.
Knowledge of power factor issues and solutions.
Ability to perform basic estimating procedures.
Comprehensive understanding of transformers, motors, variable frequency drives, and load characteristics.
Proficiency in lighting design and protection systems​.

Recommended Credentials
Customer Experience Level 1
Jobsite Safety Level 1
Personal Safety Level 1
Installation Level 1
Lockout/Tagout​.
Personal Development Level 1
Troubleshooting Level 1
Project Documentation Level 1​.
Professional Development Level 1
Safety Documentation Level 1
Autodesk Build Level 1​.
Leadership Development Level 1
Advanced Safety Practices​.

Title: Apprentice - Second Year
Description:
Apprentice Electrician - Second Year
What Does a Second-Year Apprentice Do?
In their second year, apprentices gain more hands-on experience with larger electrical systems and complex wiring setups. They learn to read blueprints, install larger conduit systems, and perform basic motor control installations. They also start developing a deeper understanding of electrical theories and safety practices.
What Skills Are Required?
Ability to install rigid conduits using hand benders.
Skills to wire basic motor controls such as start/stop switches.
Capability to read and interpret blueprints for circuit information.
Experience pulling wire up to 4/0 MCM and installing conduits up to 2 inches.
Understanding of AC waveforms, inductance, capacitance, power factor, and voltage drops.
Hooking up single-phase and three-phase loads​.
Recommended Credentials
Customer Experience Level 1
Jobsite Safety Level 1
Personal Safety Level 1
Installation Level 1
Lockout/Tagout​.
Personal Development Level 1
Troubleshooting Level 1
Project Documentation Level 1​.

Title: Apprentice - Third Year
Description:
Apprentice Electrician - Third Year
What Does a Third-Year Apprentice Do?
In the third year, apprentices expand their skills in handling larger projects, including advanced conduit installations and high-voltage electrical systems. They are expected to be proficient in reading electrical drawings and applying the National Electrical Code (NEC) to ensure safe and compliant installations.
What Skills Are Required?
Proficiency in installing all sizes of conduit systems.
Ability to rig and pull all types and sizes of wire and cable.
Detailed understanding of NEC for selecting proper conductors, calculating conduit fill, box fill, and grounding sizes.
Ability to wire up motor controls and perform high-voltage terminations (5 kV – 15 kV).
Skilled in using multi-meters and meggers for system testing​.
Recommended Credentials
Customer Experience Level 1
Jobsite Safety Level 1
Personal Safety Level 1
Installation Level 1
Lockout/Tagout​.
Personal Development Level 1
Troubleshooting Level 1
Project Documentation Level 1​.
Professional Development Level 1
Safety Documentation Level 1
Autodesk Build Level 1​.

Title: Apprentice Electrician
Description: 3.2.1APPRENTICE ELECTRICIANElectrical apprentices learn the trade through a combination of field experience, classroom work (either in class or internet), and lab work.  Although licensing requirements vary by state, typically, electrical apprentices must complete 8,000 hours of on-the-job field experience, eight semesters of apprentice course work and lab work, and pass the journeyman exam to become a licensed journeyman electrician.SKILL LEVELS:Listed below are the anticipated skill levels for first, second, third- and fourth-year electrical apprentices.  These skill levels are obtained through a combination of apprenticeship course work and on-the-job work experience.  The order in which these skills are obtained will vary depending on the opportunities available on construction projects.  Typical First Year Apprentice Skills (End of Year)1.	Working knowledge of D.C. calculations and relationships.OHMS LawPower EquationManipulate equations to solve for variables.  Explain these concepts in common terms.2.	Working knowledge of batteries and sources of electrical energy.3.	Know nominal AC voltages- single phase and three phase.4.	Familiarity with names of a wide variety of electrical parts and their ordering criteria.5.	Understand panel boards and their general layout including system grounds and equipment grounds.6.	Ability to bend and install EMT conduit with hand benders.7.	Use continuity testers, ammeters with safe practices.8.	Set up and pull wire and cable up to #2.9.	Understand 3 way and 4 way switching schemes.Typical Second Year Apprentice Skills (End of Year)1.	Ability to install rigid conduit with hand benders.2.	Wire up simple motor controls (i.e. stop/start).3.	Find circuit and other information on blueprints.4.	Rig and pull wire up to 4/0 MCM.5.	Installation of all conduit systems up to 2".6.	Understand and be able to explain AC wave form.7.	Understand and explain the following terms/concepts.1.	Inductance2.	Capacitance3.	Power factor4.	Voltage drop5.	KVA and KW8.	Hook-up single phase and 3 phase loads properly.9.	Basic knowledge of overcurrent protection.10.	Read blueprint elevations and details meaningfully.11.	Have a basic familiarity with transformers.Typical Third Year Apprenticeship Skills (End of Year)1.	Ability to install all sizes of conduit systems.2.	Rig and pull all types and sizes of wire and cable.3.	Demonstrate knowledge of N.E.C. (National Electric Code)a.	Select proper size conductor.b.	Calculate conduit fillc.	Calculate box fill/gutter fill/etc.d.	Calculate grounding conductor sizes properly.e.	Select overcurrent protection properly.4.	Read risers, schedules, details, evaluations and plan view drawings accurately and cross reference between electrical/mechanical/architectural drawings.5.	Demonstrate proper use of multi-meters, meggars, and other testers.6.	Understand and wire up motor controls and simple instruments.7.	Make 5 KV - 15 KV terminations and splices and understand high voltage safety considerations.8.	Set/terminate/start-up 600 V and 5 KV - 15 KV gear, transformers, capacitors, motors.Typical Fourth Year Apprenticeship Skills (End of Year)1.	Advanced motor control and instrument hook-up.2.	Understand classified and hazardous installation including wiring methods, equipment characteristics, and safety considerations.3.	Understand and install UPS (uninterruptable power supply) and similar components. 4.	Understand harmonics, power factor, problems and how to test for, recognize and treat them.5.	Understand basic estimating procedures.6.	Comprehensive understanding of transformers, motors, variable frequency drives and other typical loads.7.	Understand differences in light sourcesa.	efficiencyb.	color renditionc.	heat dissipationd.	layout and basic design8.	Understand basic lightning protection.9.	Service, feeder, branch circuit differences, calculations, and definitions.10.	Demand factors, de-rating calculations and procedures for panel boards, conductors, transformer loads.11.	Familiarity with overhead line components and configurations.12.	Familiarity with intrinsically safe circuits and components.All apprentices must study and follow GSL’s safety policies, produce high quality work, achieve satisfactory production rates, apply lean construction principles, work as a team player, and be willing to be mentored by Journeyman, Leadmen, and higher levels of GSL leadership.

Title: Board of Directors
Description: 7.4.8  BOARD OF DIRECTORSThe GSL Board of Directors is the company’s highest leadership body. Therefore, the Board of Directors and its individual members are fiduciaries of GSL Electric.A fiduciary is a person and/or group that acts on behalf of the company, putting the company’s interest ahead of their own, with a duty to preserve good faith and trust. Being a fiduciary thus requires being bound both legally and ethically to act in the company’s best interests.All board members must understand and commit to certain legally imposed fiduciary duties. There are three such duties. They are the duty of care, duty of loyalty, and duty of obedience. Each one is unique and critical to the success of the company, and failure to fulfill any of these duties may expose the individual to personal liability. Duty of Care — Each board member has a legal responsibility to participate actively in making decisions on behalf of the company and to exercise his or her best judgment while doing so. Board members are to exercise the care, diligence, and skill to make decisions that are financially, ethically, legally sound, and with a good faith belief that their decisions are in the best interest of the company.Duty of Loyalty — Each board member must put the interests of the company before their personal and professional interests, or the interest of others, when acting on behalf of the company in a decision-making capacity. Duty of Obedience — Board members bear the legal responsibility of ensuring that the company complies with the applicable federal, state, ad local laws and adheres to its mission.Responsibilities of the GSL Board of Directors - The GSL Board of Directors will support the work of the company and provide mission-based leadership and strategic governance. GSL Electric’s Board of Directors sets the Company’s strategic plan.  GSL’s Corporate Officers and the Executive Committee lead the day-to-day operations of the Company.  GSL Electric’s Board of Directors, GSL’s Corporate Officers, and GSL’s Executive Committee form a management partnership. Appropriate leadership by GSL’s Board of Directors is both critical and expected. The GSL Board of Directors responsibilities are (but not limited to):Govern GSL Electric in accordance with its culture including its objective, vision, mission, and core values as identified in Section 1.3 of GSL’s Policies and Procedures.Select and appoint the Executive Officers to whom responsibility for the administration of the company is delegated.Review and evaluate the Executive Officers’ performance based on a specific job description, including the leadership in the company, in strategic and program planning and implementation, and in the management of the company and its personnel.Provide proper financial oversight.Ensure legal compliance and ethical integrity.Manage resources responsibly.Strive for continual improvement of the company’s operations, programs, policies, and services.Assessing its own performance as the governing body of the company.Attend four quarterly Board of Directors Meetings.Attend Special Board of Directors Meetings, Strategic Planning Sessions, etc.Develop and approve a strategic plan and ensure that it is followed.Address hrs attending meetings, expenses – no loss of payResponsibilities of the Chairman of the Board -The Chairman of the Board is appointed by the Board of Directors and is responsible to set the board’s agenda and facilitate board meetings.  The Chairman of the Board must have a good understanding of the day-to-day operations and management of the company. Responsibilities of Individual Board Members -To ensure that the Board of Directors is making the best decisions. Board members are to exercise the care, diligence, and skill to make decisions that are financially, ethically, and legally sound.  Therefore, the responsibilities of individual board members include (but not limited to) the following:Be aware of the GSL's objective, vision, mission, core values, strategic plans, and policies and procedures. The board member must also ensure that the strategic plans and policies serve the needs of the company.Understand substantive matters brought before the board.Prepare for and participate fully in board meetings, deliberations, and decisions. This involves preparing for and attending meetings, asking questions, challenging assumptions, following up on issues that may not have been resolved, and consulting with experts as needed.  Planning your workRead, evaluate, and ensure the accuracy of all reports. This includes minutes, financial reports, and evaluations.Participate in the evaluation of business operations and executives.Maintain confidentiality on all internal organizational affairs, including all board discussions, topics, and/or decisions. The appropriate information will be made available to GSL Employee-Owners through designated channels.Board members are to support and advocate the final decision(s) made by the board.Serve as active advocates and ambassadors of GSL Electric and fully engage in supporting GSL’s Employee-Owners, and in identifying and securing the financial resources and partnerships necessary for the organization to advance its mission.All new members of the Board of Directors shall go through training as determined by the Board.

Title: Corporate Officers
Description: 7.4.7CORPORATE OFFICERSChief Executive Officer - The Chief Executive Officer (CEO) reports to GSL Electric’s Board of Directors.  The CEO leads GSL’s Executive Committee and works with the committee to align the culture of the company with GSL’s Objective, Vision, Mission, and Values Statement and in executing GSL’s Communications Plan.The CEO works with the Executive Committee to review and provide annual updates to GSL’s Business Model, Five Year Plan, and Plan of Succession, that is approved and ratified by GSL’s Board of Directors.The CEO adheres to GSL’s Corporate Bylaws and all aspects of proper corporate governance.The CEO works with the Executive Committee to develop and implement all compensation plans for the company.The CEO chairs the Business Policy Committee and oversees the development of policies and procedures that are consistent with GSL’s values, meets the needs of the company, maintains compliance with federal and state laws, and provides guidance to help achieve the company’s goals and objectives.  	The CEO develops a successful risk management program to protect the interests of the company and its Employee-Owners.  Risk Management includes overseeing GSL’s insurance programs, development, and training on GSL’s Management Directives, and overseeing GSL’s Contract Manager performance in the company. The CEO serves as the Plan Administrator and Trustee for GSL’s Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP) and its 401k Profit Sharing Plan.  The CEO serves as the Chairman of GSL’s Board of Directors and provides communications to GSL’s Board of Directors and GSL’s investor group on a quarterly basis.   The CEO conducts the Company’s quarterly Progress Meetings.  The CEO promotes communication to its employees by overseeing the presentation and content of the Employee-Owner monthly newsletter and visiting job sites 5% regularly to see how our Employee/Owners are doing and to express appreciation for their services.PresidentThe President supports the CEO in attaining the goals and objectives set forth by GSL’s Board of Directors.  Although the President can oversee and assist in all aspects of GSL’s business activities, the President has primary responsibility for all marketing and business development activities of the company while focusing on the development of the culture of the company.  Business development is the leadership function that ensures a sustainable business future for GSL Electric through the continuous improvement of its processes and services to better meet the needs of current and future customers. The President works with the Executive Committee, Branch Managers, Business Development Officers, Project Managers, Estimators, Engineers, and Department Managers to develop and train all personnel involved in the marketing and business development efforts of the company. The President is responsible to develop and maintain a marketing and business development plan and the corresponding budget.  The President is responsible to execute the plan and ensure that the expenses stay within the budget that has been approved by the Executive Committee.The President takes the lead in proposal management when a Branch Business Development Officer is not appointed to perform this responsibility.The President is responsible for implementing ongoing updates to GSL’s web site, issuing quarterly client newsletters, conducting, and analyzing the results of Employee/Owner surveys, and controlling all of GSL’s marketing materials and initiatives including pre-qualifications and the development and availability of department line cards. The President leads the Marketing and Business Development Committee and oversees the Corporate Marketing Manager position.The President oversees the marketing and the budget of the company store offerings to Employee/Owners as approved by GSL’s Executive Committee.The President visits job sites regularly to see how our Employee/Owners are doing and to express appreciation for their services.The President oversees GSL’s safety program and supervises GSL’s Safety Director.Currently, the President serves as the Contract Manager for GSL’s Las Vegas Branch.  A Contract Manager reviews and summarizes designated executed prime contracts and executed first-tier electrical contracts; prepares Contract Summaries; and conducts a review of the Contract Summary with Project Managers & Project Foreman.  The Contract Manager provides notices as required under the terms of the contracts and provides additional managerial oversight as necessary to support successful project outcomes. Chief Operations Officer (COO)The COO supports the CEO in attaining the goals and objectives set forth by GSL’s Board of Directors.    The COO has full responsibility and accountability for all field operations including Project Start-Up, Pre-Construction, Pre-Fabrication, Project Performance, and Project Closeout.   The COO develops Standard Operating Procedures (SOP’s) & ensures implementation of GSL’s Standard Operating Procedures.The COO develops and updates GSL’s field operation leadership training plan and provides consistent training and development opportunities for field operation’s leadership.  In addition to monthly Foremen/Project Management training, the training plan is to include formal course development and training with Certifications for multi-step Lead Men, Foremen, Superintendents, Project Coordinators, and Project Managers.  The COO supports implementation of GSL’s Management Directives relating to field operations.The COO is responsible for achieving operational performance objectives by monitoring and controlling GSL’s field operations utilizing GSL’s Job Plan and other management tools.The COO is an advocate for lean construction techniques focusing on continual improvement.  The COO monitors GSL’s current manpower and leadership needs and monitors the quality and performance of GSL’s work force and GSL’s field leadership, assesses employee morale and ensures proper safety program implementation.The COO identifies future manpower and leadership needs and develops a plan to meet those needs.The COO leads the Operations Committee and oversees the Best Practices Committee in developing GSL’s SOP’s.  The COO works with Branch Managers to develop and oversee GSL’s Pre-Fabrication program.The COO visits job sites regularly to monitor effective pre-planning of the work, assess equipment and resource needs, reviews labor production.  The COO maintains a concentrated focus on the training and development of our field operations team. The COO oversees the company’s electrical contractor licenses in each state in which we do business.Chief Financial Officer (CFO)The CFO directs the business management / business administration team.  Such duties include the following:  The CFO generates GSL’s monthly WIP Reports, Performance Analysis, and GSL’s interim Financial Statements;  The CFO updates GSL’s Executive Committee, Branch Management, and Project Management regarding financial performance and benchmark performance;The CFO secures a sufficient banking line of credit, submits required reports to the bank on a timely basis, and maintains positive banking relationships; 	The CFO secures a bonding capacity sufficient to meet the needs of the company, submits required reports to GSL’s bonding agent on timely basis, and maintains positive relationships with GSL’s agent and surety;The CFO develops and maintains viable insurance programs for GSL’s health and welfare benefits, and coverage for workers compensation, property and casualty, general liability, umbrella, professional liability, short term and long-term disability, buy/sell agreements, etc. 	The CFO supervises GSL’s general ledger, payroll, accounts payable, and accounts receivable accounting functions;  The CFO is responsible to monitor cash flows, take eligible cash discounts, maximize interest income, minimize interest expenses, and manage the cash investments of the company; The CFO establishes and oversees the administration of GSL’s fringe benefit programs and GSL’s Flex Spending Plan.The CFO oversees all financial audits, submits Annual Reports, and insures local, state, and federal tax compliance.Vice-PresidentsCorporate Secretary

Description: 7.3.4ENGINEERING / DESIGNCAD and REVIT OperatorsCAD and REVIT operators may be needed to assist designers in the production of the electrical drawings required on a project.  CAD and REVIT operators may also be used to assist in BIM modeling for a project.  CAD and REVIT operators work under the direction of designers, estimators, and engineers to produce quality drawings that minimize the amount of field engineering that is be required.EstimatorsEstimators are assigned to the following departments: estimating, special projects, low voltage, and design build.  Estimators are to follow GSL’s estimating policies and procedures and work under the direction of their Department Managers and Branch Managers.   The goal of estimators is to help procure work of sufficient volume and level of profitability to help their branch office achieve their annual goals and objectives.  Estimators must produce quality bids that have complete and accurate pricing.  Final pricing shall be determined by Branch Managers when considering the labor risk ratio, overhead and profit parameters, the need for work, and issues relative to the individual projects.  When possible, Estimators are to work with GSL’s Marketing Manager and GSL’s Branch Business Development Officer to customize the narrative for each individual estimate submitted.DesignersDesigners may be needed to assist GSL Engineers in the completion of details of the design.  Designers shall work under the direction of GSL’s Engineer and shall coordinate with operations on constructability issues.  Designers are tasked with issuing as complete of a design as possible to facilitate efficiencies in the electrical construction of the project. EngineersGSL shall retain on staff a licensed Electrical Professional Engineer to submit proposals, complete the design, and stamp drawings on work procured in the western United States for GSL Electric.  The Engineer shall work closely with GSL’s business development team to find solid opportunities for the design build department.  The full scope of the design shall be determined through the RFI process and the proposal shall offer minimal exclusions.  For scope that is not able to be ascertained and quantified, a qualified allowance may be offered as an estimate of the anticipated costs based on our experience.  Deductive alternates may also be offered if applicable.  Engineers are to work with GSL’s Marketing Manager and GSL’s Business Development Officer to customize the narrative for each individual proposal submitted.

Description: 7.3.3ESTIMATINGEstimatorsEstimators are assigned to the following departments: estimating, special projects, low voltage, and design build.  Estimators are to follow GSL’s estimating policies and procedures and work under the direction of their Department Manager and Branch Manager.   The goal of Estimators is to help procure work of sufficient volume and level of profitability to help their branch office achieve their annual goals and objectives.  Estimators must produce quality bids that have complete and accurate pricing.  Final pricing shall be determined by Branch Managers when considering the labor risk, overhead and profit parameters, the need for work, and issues relative to the individual projects.  When possible, Estimators are to work with GSL’s Marketing Manager and GSL’s Branch Business Development Officer to customize the narrative for each individual estimate submitted.Estimators should always follow GSL’s Estimating Management Directives.ESTIMATING JOB DESCRIPTIONSLEVEL I ESTIMATOR ASSISTANTJob Duties & Key Responsibilities include but are not limited to the descriptions below.  It should be noted that this list is subject to change at any time and may be modified as necessary as conditions and needs dictate:SKILL SETAny level of field experience is definitely preferred.Basic Outlook, Word and Excel skills are a must.Must have the ability to write “professionally” using proper English.Must be able to present yourself professionally in a business setting.  Be able to take direction from the Estimators you are working for and follow through on commitments made.A Level I Estimator will be expected to enroll in Apprenticeship Training classes unless already attending classes.  Begin to develop a level of understanding of NEC.Good communication skills.Be a “Team Player”.Most important is a good attitude and the ability to work well with others and the ability to follow direction and learn from Estimators you are working for.You will not be required or expected to use Accubid as a Level I Estimator Assistant.  However, it will be up to you to learn as much as possible about the estimating process in general and to pick-up whatever you can about Accubid as you are doing your job.  Basically, if you want to continue on and become an Estimator, you will need to show the ability and drive needed to be given additional duties/responsibilities.  BID RESPONSBILITIES – Essentially, the role of the Level I Estimator is to count devices, fixtures etc.Follow direction given to you by Estimators.   These tasks may include items such as: Downloading drawings from websites,Printing drawings,Making job folders, Preparing drawing sets for different Estimators working on a project,Responding to e-mails regarding bid inquiries etc. It is assumed that a Level I Estimator Assistant does not comprehend what is being represented on the drawings and is not at a level where they can accurately interpret this information.  A Level I Estimator Assistant shall only “roll lengths” once he has proven that he has the capacity to complete this task accurately.  Not all Level I Estimator Assistants will “roll lengths”. This assumption is to be maintained until proven otherwise and Chief Estimator gives the approval for the Level I Estimator Assistant to “roll lengths” or perform any other duties other than count and color.  Even if the Level I Estimator Assistant is cleared to “roll lengths” for one project, he may not be cleared to do the same on a different project due to the type of job or job complexity etc.  The Level I Estimator Assistant is to communicate with vendors/subs only as directed by Estimators.  A Level I Estimator Assistant is an entry level position and it will be up to the individual to demonstrate to Estimators the capability to progress further and become an actual Estimator.   ESTIMATING JOB DESCRIPTIONSLEVEL II INTERMEDIATE ESTIMATORJob Duties & Key Responsibilities include but are not limited to the descriptions below.  It should be noted that this list is subject to change at any time and may be modified as necessary as conditions and needs dictate:SKILL SET – Must have some experience in bidding electrical work.Proficient general computer skills are a must.Proficient in use of Outlook, Excel and Word is a must.A reasonable level of field experience is preferred.A beginner to mid-level of proficiency in Accubid is required for a Level II Estimator. Your level of proficiency in Accubid will depend upon your time as a Level II Estimator. You will be expected to continually improve in Accubid as time passes.Beginning to gain an understanding of NECA rates and how the labor rates are established in Accubid.Must have the ability to write “professionally” using proper English and industry correct terms.Must have good communication skills.Working knowledge of NEC.  A level II Estimator is expected to be actively enrolled in Apprenticeship Training unless all 4 years have previously been completed.  It is expected that once Apprenticeship training is completed, you will get your Journeyman License.Must be able to present yourself professionally in a business setting and be prepared to dress appropriately when meeting with clients.Most important isA good attitude and the ability to work well with othersThe ability to teach/mentor Level I Estimators.Be able to take direction from Chief Estimator, Lead EstimatorFollow through on commitments made. Be a “Team Player”.ASSESS RISK OF PROJECT – While executing tasks assigned to you by the Level III Lead Estimator you are working for, it is your responsibility to make note of, document and make the Lead Estimator aware of anything that relates to the risk of the project. This may include but is not limited to items such as;Identifying incomplete design drawings or errors/omissions in the design of the drawings that will cause us to take on risk one way or another if we bid the project. These items cause us to take on risk because if the design is incomplete or if there are errors in the design, we must make certain assumptions or choose a method to address them that will put a level of risk on GSL when our bid gets submitted.  KNOW FRONT-END DOCUMENTS –As a Level II Estimator, it is not your responsibility to figure out what the Front-End Documents are specifying, however it is your responsibility to get this information from your Lead Estimator and bid the job accordingly.  If you have a question, ask the question.  Do not assume you know the answer.  Do not assume it is a stupid question.  Err on the side of caution.  Trust your Lead Estimator and use him as a resource.  WORK WITH VENDORS/SUBS – Work with the vendors/subs your Lead Estimator asks you to work with.Work on developing your relationship with these contacts at all times and your relationship to gain information about the job and about our competition that can help us be more competitive.Maintain contact with vendors/subs throughout project to make sure they are going to come through for us on bid day.Be careful not to give away information to vendors/subs that they could pass on to our competition that could harm us.Work to assemble quotes as they arrive and present documents to Lead Estimator so he can easily review information. Save quotes in estimate file along with other project documentation.MAINTAIN GSL PROJECT DOCUMENTATION – Develop estimate folder complete with all folders and documents needed for estimate.Create estimate number for project and let other members of estimating team know when the folder is ready and what the estimate number is.Enter and maintain all project information in CRM system.Download, print and incorporate drawing changes/addenda etc. Make sure all changes get passed on to appropriate parties, vendors, subs etc.Document questions/concerns in estimate folder and consult with Lead Estimator as to whether RFI’s need to be submitted or if it can be addressed by Lead Estimator.Maintain list of clarifications, inclusions and exclusions on Proposal letter with input of Lead Estimator.Document all RFI’s submitted and answers received or not received.Be prepared to discuss any issues that were not fully answered or clarified through RFI process during bid review. Work with Lead Estimator to properly document and address all concerns as they arise throughout bid.EXECUTE “TAKE-OFF GAME-PLAN” – Prior to any actual take-off being done, sit down with Lead Estimator for the project and he will layout our “strategy” or “game-plan” for  how to take-off the project in the manner that will give us the best chance of capturing the work.  It is crucial that the take-off be done as directed by Lead Estimator.  You may not fully understand or agree with methodology of Lead Estimator but in order to avoid mistakes we must all be on the same page when the take-off gets performed. Check scale on each drawing prior to rolling. After determining proper scale of drawing, write on layout drawing what scale you are using and initial next to it so it can be clearly visible when checking what scale was used when rolling lengths. Use labor factoring when appropriate and where directed by Lead Estimator. Work with Lead Estimator to improve your skills with Accubid and general estimating skills.  SUPERVISE LEVEL I ESTIMATORS –As a Level II Estimator it is part of your job to supervise and help Level I Estimators with their work.  You should have mastered all tasks being performed by a Level I Estimator therefore, he should not need to go to the Lead Estimator to get all of his questions answered.  You can consult with your Lead Estimator about a question brought to you by the Level I Estimator if you need assurance that you are answering the question correctly.  You will be responsible for the work done of a Level I Estimator if you are both working on the same project.If you feel that a particular Estimator is not at the level he needs to be,Spend the necessary time to train them so that you can gain the level of trust needed.Check up on their progress at regular intervals so any mistakes get caught as soon as possible.  	 Do not wait until the bid review and have someone else catch an obvious mistake that never should have happened.Make sure the Level I Estimators feel comfortable asking questions and seeking out your advice. Be a mentor, teach and treat the Level I Estimators the way you would want to be taught and treated if you were in their shoes.Help Level I Estimators understand how our system works. Training and teaching Level I Estimators is part of your job.MAINTAIN TEAM ATTITUDE –In order for GSL to be successful, all aspects of the business must be successful.  As Estimators, we rely on the Operations group to successfully execute the projects we win.  We need to develop an attitude of trust and respect not only among each other in the estimating department but also with the other branches of GSL, in particular the Operations group.  Estimating is a service to OperationsWe are not benefitting anyone if we land projects that Operations cannot support or if we win projects that were not bid properly and never have a chance to be successful.  We must always maintain an open mind and be ready and willing to learn from each other.As a Level II Estimator, your attitude and your willingness to work with others is critical to the atmosphere and the success of the department and the company.The Level I Estimators will rely on you for help and training.The Lead Estimators will rely on you to execute the take-off accurately and correctly in order for the job to be successful. The Operations group will notice your attitude and any reason they can get to blame you for their job not going well, they will take especially if they perceive you to be of the attitude that “Well, we got the job now it’s your responsibility to make it work!”  Be a positive/motivational leader and a team player.Work to develop the trust of your Lead Estimator.BID REVIEWS – By the time the project gets to the point of being reviewed by Branch Manager and/or other corporate officers the Level II Estimator needs to “own” the portion of the project that you were responsible for.All questions should be able to be answered clearly and confidently. You should be able to explain exactly why you included or didn’t include what you did in the estimate. You should never reveal any surprises or information in the bid review that you haven’t already discussed with your Lead Estimator. This does not mean you should withhold information if you suddenly realize there is an issue that hasn’t been addressed. If there is something that needs to be discussed that hasn’t been addressed then we have to address it. The intent of this statement is to try and resolve all issues prior to getting to the bid review.The goal is to present the job to Branch Managers/Corporate with the most accurate representation of true cost to build the job.  The best way a Level II Estimator can do this is by showing that you accurately followed the direction of your Lead Estimator and you know your portion of the project “inside and out” so that we don’t leave anyone feeling uneasy about the information we are presenting in the bid review.BID DAY RESPONSBILITIES – Work with vendors to get Bills of Materials prior to bid day to review scope/counts etc. Work with vendors to make sure all quotes are going to arrive on time. Organize and file all quotes in job folder. Have all quote/bid information organized and ready for easy access by Lead Estimator. Prior to bid, make a list of all parties the bid needs to be sent to and have this ready so there is not any confusion when the number needs to be submitted. Work with Lead Estimator to ensure Proposal Letter is finalized and complete.Work with Lead Estimator to make sure everyone received our number.Once job is awardedIt is not your job to inform vendors who was low or where there numbers were in comparison to their competition.Even though vendor “ABC” may be 1% lower than vendor “XYZ”, that does not mean they are going to be awarded the job.Estimators should never inform vendors/subs that they have won a job with us.Operations decides who to award the jobs to, not estimating.  When asked by vendors/subs how their numbers looked or if they got the job, all that needs to be said is that they can talk to whoever the PM is going to be and he will let them know.ESTIMATING JOB DESCRIPTIONSLEVEL III LEAD ESTIMATORJob Duties & Key Responsibilities include but are not limited to the descriptions below.  It should be noted that this list is subject to change at any time and may be modified as necessary as conditions and needs dictate:SKILL SET –Be able to take direction from Chief Estimator and follow through on commitments made.Proficient general computer skills are a must.Proficient in use of Outlook, Excel and Word is a must.A high level of proficiency in Accubid is a must for a Level III Lead Estimator.  You must not only be able to use it efficiently and correctly but you must be able to teach Level I and II Estimators how to use it as well.Must have a good understanding of NECA rates and how the labor rates are established in Accubid.Must have the ability to write “professionally” using proper English and industry correct terms.Good communication skills.Working knowledge of NEC.  Completed Apprenticeship Training Program and/or Journeyman License.  Journeyman level knowledge of means/methods of installation.  Preferably holds a current Journeyman license.Must be able to present yourself professionally in a business setting and be prepared to dress appropriately when meeting with clients.Must have experience in bidding all types of electrical work.Most important is a good attitude and the ability to work well with others and the ability to teach/mentor Level I and II Estimators. Be an effective leader.  ASSESS RISK OF PROJECT –Work with Chief Estimator to assess viability of project for company. This is a detailed process that must be covered thoroughly for every job.  It is the duty of a Level III Lead Estimator to determine:project schedulemanpower requirementswho the competition iswhat type of bid it is (Lump Sum / Time & Material / GMP / T&M NTE etc.).The Level III Lead Estimator along with the Chief Estimator must be able to explain in detail to Corporate and Branch Officers what the potential Risk vs. Reward is for each project they are assigned to.KNOW FRONT-END DOCUMENTS – Carefully read through and address all items in the front-end documents.This includes determining material/gear/lighting etc. requirements of the specifications.Determine if alternates can be used to gain a competitive advantage against competition.Identify all project deadlines (i.e. when do we have to submit RFI’s by, bid deadline etc.)Identify all scope/cost items in narrative form that are not necessarily shown on layout drawings. For example:Third Party Testing RequirementsSafety RequirementsQA/QC RequirementsFireproofing, Seismic RequirementsChange Order Opportunities, etc.Is Bid Bond or P&P Bond required?Are we required to submit a schedule with our bid?Is there a specific bid form that must be used?Do we have to submit rates with our bid?Do we have to submit unit rates with bid and if so for what purpose will they be used?  What are we agreeing to when we submit our bid?For example, many RFQ/RFP packages that we get are the actual Contract Documents and when we fill out these forms and submit them with our bids we are agreeing to the entire contract “as is”.  This can potentially be very damaging.WORK WITH VENDORS/SUBS –Make contact with all required vendors/subs on project.  Work to see if any particular vendor/sub has “inside track” or any type of advantage that would cause us to want to favor one particular vendor/sub over another. Let vendors/subs know what other Estimators are working on the project with you. Firmly establish deadlines for when you need quotes and other information submitted to you. Constantly work to improve GSL’s relationship and reputation with vendors/subs.Keep in contact with vendors/subs throughout duration of project to ensure everything can be submitted as planned so there are no surprises on bid day. Use relationship with our vendors/subs to gain information about our competition such as who else is bidding the project etc.DEVELOP GSL PROJECT DOCUMENTATION – Immediately begin project “Proposal Letter”.Maintain list of clarifications, inclusions and exclusions on letter.Develop RFI log and submit RFI’s as necessary.Be prepared to discuss any issues that were not fully answered or clarified through RFI process so that everyone in bid review has complete understanding of the risk and corporate/branch leadership can determine how to handle the situation. Work with Level I and II Estimators to make sure all of their issues and concerns get captured in Proposal Letter, RFI’s etc.ESTABLISH “TAKE-OFF GAME-PLAN” – Prior to any actual take-off being done:Sit down with other Estimators who will be involved with project and layout your “strategy” or “game-plan” for how to take-off the project in the manner that will give us the best chance of capturing the work.It may be advantageous to involve a PM and/or Foreman in this process who are familiar with this type of work. Determine if there is any possibility of pre-manufacturing/pre-fabrication that can be utilized on the project.Discuss areas where labor factoring could be used and areas where it must be used. Discuss how the breakout in Accubid needs to be setup.Make sure that estimating team has clear vision of how to move forward and what their roles are in the project.Ensure that estimating checklist gets filled out and addressed during bidding process.SUPERVISE LEVEL I AND II ESTIMATORS – As lead Estimator it will be your job to utilize the Level I and II Estimators in the manner most efficient for your project.If you feel that a particular Estimator is not at the level he needs to be, spend the necessary time to train them so that you can gain the level of trust needed. Check up on their progress at regular intervals so any mistakes get caught as soon as possible. Do not wait until the bid review and have someone else catch an obvious mistake that never should have happened.Make sure the other Estimators feel comfortable asking questions and seeking out your advice.Be a mentor, teach and treat the Level I and II Estimators the way you would want to be taught and treated if you were in their shoes.Help Level I and II Estimators understand how Accubid works and why we do what we do in Accubid.Training and teaching Level I and II Estimators is part of your job.MAINTAIN TEAM ATTITUDE – In order for GSL to be successful, all aspects of the business must be successful.  As Estimators, we rely on the Operations group to successfully execute the projects we win.  We need to develop an attitude of trust and respect not only among each other in the estimating department but also with the other branches of GSL, in particular the Operations group.  Estimating is a service to Operations.  We are not benefitting anyone if we land projects that Operations cannot support or if we win projects that were not bid properly and never have a chance to be successful.  We must always maintain an open mind and be ready and willing to learn from each other.As a Level III Lead Estimator, your attitude and your willingness to work with others is critical to the atmosphere and the success of the department and the company.  The other Estimators will follow your lead and if you have a good attitude, so will they and vice-versa.  The Operations group will notice your attitude and any reason they can get to blame you for their job not going well, they will take especially if they perceive you to be of the attitude that “Well, we got the job now it’s your responsibility to make it work!”Be a positive/motivational leader and a team player.BID REVIEWS –By the time the project gets to the point of being reviewed by Branch Manager and/or other Corporate officers the Level III Lead Estimator needs to “own” the project.All questions should be able to be answered clearly and confidently.You should be able to explain exactly why you included or didn’t include what you did in the estimate.  At this point, there is no reason to blame Level I and II Estimators for what has been done. The goal is to present the job to Branch Managers/Corporate with the most accurate representation of actual cost to build the job.It is then up to them if they wish to cut margin or otherwise manipulate numbers to change the value of the bid.Your job is to present what you see as the actual cost to build the job.Ensure bid review checklist gets utilized on every bid.BID DAY RESPONSBILITIES – Prior to bid day, make and maintain contact with all GC’s/Owners we are bidding to. Find out who we need to be directing questions to and who the “key” person is that we need to be working with.Ask questions to see if there is anything we can provide that would give us an edge or anything we can do to separate ourselves from the competition.After the bid is submitted:Follow-up with all GC’s or owners we bid to and make sure they got our number and ask for feedback.Probe for information regarding where we stand and if there is anything we can do or if there is anything else they need from us.Once job is awarded, it is not your job to inform vendors who was low or where there numbers were in comparison to their competition.Even though vendor “ABC” may be 1% lower than vendor “XYZ”, that does not mean they are going to be awarded the job.Operations decides who to award the jobs to, not estimating.When asked by vendors/subs how their numbers looked or if they got the job, all that needs to be said is that they can talk to whoever the PM is going to be and he will let them know.Estimators should never inform vendors/subs that they have won a job with us.

Title: Foreman
Description: 3.2.4FOREMANSelection of GSL Electric Foreman is a function of the needs of the company, the Employee/Owner's education, knowledge, skills, experience, competency, and performance.  Responsibilities of a Foreman include but are not limited to the following:1.	All functions of a GSL Journeyman Electrician.2.	Completion of all requirements to achieve certification as a GSL Safety Coordinator including current certification in Standard First Aid and Adult CPR.3.	Production control, quality control and cost control over assigned work areas.4. 	Implementation of lean construction principles.5.	Full implementation of GSL's Safety and Loss Control Program at the Foreman level, including direct responsibility for a crew's safety and enforcement of all company policies and procedures.6.	Training, protecting, directing, and managing Employee/Owners over whom you are assigned.7.	Protecting the interests of GSL Electric by insuring all Employee/Owners represent the company in a manner that represents the highest ethical behavior, and proper dress, grooming, speech, and professional conduct.8.	Knowledge and utilization of all GSL standard operating procedures such as estimating, job set-up/close out, job plans, purchase orders, scheduling, reports, contract status, time cards, time card summaries, tool control, work vouchers, etc.9.	Plan, schedule, train, follow through and promote teamwork to accomplish the company's objective of achieving profitable operations through safety, quality, and productivity.See the Foreman Job Description Below -Job Title: FOREMANDepartment: OperationsSupervisor: Project Manager / General ForemanThe selection of a GSL Electric foreman is a function based on the needs of the company, the employee’s education, knowledge, skills, experience, competency and performance.  Qualifications: Journeyman or Masters License or equivalent education and experience. Certification as a GSL Safety Coordinator, including current certification in Standard First Aid and Adult CPR. Current state issued Driver’s License. OSHA 30 may also be required in some states. To perform the job successfully, an individual must be able to perform each essential duty satisfactorily. The requirements listed below are representative of the knowledge, skill and/or ability required. Reasonable accommodations may be made to enable individuals with disabilities to perform the essential functions.Summary: Directly supervise 7 to 10 employees in the Field Operations for the installation, maintenance and repair of electrical installations. Carry out supervisory responsibilities in accordance with the organization’s policies and applicable laws. Responsibilities include training employees, planning, assigning, and directing work; appraising performance; rewarding and disciplining employees; addressing complaints and resolving problems.  Primary responsibility is to bring the project in “Safely, On Time and within Budget”.Essential Duties and Responsibilities:	Include the following but are not all inclusive, other duties may be assigned.SafetyFull implementation of GSL’s Loss Control Program at the foreman level, including direct responsibility for a crew's safety and enforcement of all company policies and procedures.Hold weekly safety meetings.Protecting the interests of GSL Electric by insuring all employees represent the company in a manner that represents the highest ethical behavior, including dress, grooming, speech and professional conduct Knowledge and utilization of all GSL standard operating procedures such as disciplinary policy, estimating, job set-up/close out, job plans, purchase orders, scheduling, reports, contract status, time cards, tool control, work vouchers, etc.Understand the contract and the required change order procedures and support the PM as needed.Understand and follow the Project Specifications.Become familiar with all approved submittals and assure that what we receive from the vendors complies with the approved submittal.Integration of change orders into the scope of work.Develop and promote positive client relations.Manage the field installation for projects Become completely familiar with the project scope, site conditions, schedule and equipment being installed.Training, protecting and managing employees over whom you are assigned.Materials requisitioning, storing and staging.Plan, schedule, train, follow through and promote teamwork to accomplish the company's objective of achieving profitable operations through safety, craftsmanship and productivityMaintain a proper ratio of apprentice’s to assure that the average hourly rate is in sync with the estimate.Job Plan management. This includes updating the Project Hours to CompleteUpdate the PM weekly on the progress of the project.Maintain all field records for the projectsTime cardsSchedulesManpower ProjectionsDaily ReportsDrawingsIncorporating all:ASI’sCOR’sRFI’sAs-built informationField Labor Issues:AttendanceEnforce GSL’s Attendance PoliciesAssure GSL only pays for the hours workedAssure that breaks are not planned or organized but are used on an “as needed basis”.ProductivityPlan and facilitate the installations in an efficient mannerQualityEnsure that the materials are installed in compliance with the specifications and in a craftsman like manner therefore requiring a minimum of re-work.Training to attain the highest level of production and qualityCompetencies:	To perform the job successfully, an individual should demonstrate the following competencies:Analytical – Synthesizes complex or diverse information; collects and researches data; uses intuition and experience to complement data; designs work flows and procedures		Continuous Learning –Assesses own strengths and weaknesses; seeks feedback to improve performance’ pursues training and development opportunities; strives to continuously build knowledge and skills; shares expertise with others.	Job Knowledge -Competent in required skills and knowledge; exhibits ability to learn and apply new skills; keeps abreast of current developments; requires minimal supervision; displays understanding of how the job relates to others; uses resources effectively.		Use of Technology – Demonstrates the required skills; adapts to new technologies; troubleshoots technological problems; uses technology to increase productivity; keeps technical skills up to date.		Design – Generates creative solutions; translates concepts and information into images; uses feedback to modify designs; applies design principles; demonstrates attention to detail.		Problem Solving – Identifies and resolves problems in a timely manner; gathers and analyzes information skillfully; develops alternative solutions; works well in group problem solving situations; uses reason even when dealing with emotional topics.	Project Management – Coordinates the field operations of the project; communicates changes and progress; completes the project “Safely, On Time and within Budget”; manages the field project team activities.	Customer Service – Manage difficult or emotional customer situations; responds promptly to customer needs; solicits customer feedback to improve service; responds to request for service and assistance; meets commitments.		Communications – Expresses ideas and thoughts verbally; expresses ideas and thoughts in written forms; exhibits good listening and comprehension; keeps others adequately informed; selects and uses the appropriate communication method.		Cooperation – Establishes and maintains effective relations; exhibits tact and consideration; offers assistance and support to co-workers; works cooperatively in group situations; works actively to resolve conflict.	Teamwork –Balances team and individual responsibilities; exhibits objectivity and openness to others’ views; gives and welcomes feedback; contributes to building a positive team spirit; puts the success of the team above own interest; able to build morale and group commitments to goals and objectives; supports everyone’s’ efforts to succeed.	Change Management –Develops workable implementation plans; communicates changes effectively; builds commitment and overcomes resistance; prepares and supports those affected by change; monitors transition and evaluates results.	Performance Coaching –Defines responsibilities and expectations; sets goals and objectives; gives performance feedback; motivates for increased results; recognizes contributions; encourages training and development.		Delegation – Delegates work assignments: matched the responsibility to the person; gives authority to work independently; sets expectations and monitors delegated activities; provides recognition for results.	Leadership – Exhibits confidence in self and others; inspires and motivates others to perform well; effectively influences actions and opinions of others; accepts feedback from others; gives appropriate recognition to others.		Cost Consciousness –Works within approved budget; develops and implements cost saving measures; contributes to the profits and revenue; conserves organizational resources.		Diversity –Demonstrates knowledge of EEO policy; shows respect and sensitivity for cultural differences; educates others on the value of diversity; promotes a harassment free environment; builds a diverse workforce.		Ethics – Treats people with respect; keeps commitments; inspires the trust of others; works with integrity and principles; upholds organizational values.		Adaptability – Adapts to change in the work environment; manages competing demands; changes approach or method to best fit the situation; able to deal with frequent change, delays or unexpected events.		Personal Appearance –		Dresses appropriately for the position; and keeps well-groomed		Business Acumen –Understands business implications of decisions; displays orientation to profitability; demonstrates knowledge of market and completion; aligns work with strategic goals.		Conflict Resolution - Encourages open communication; confronts difficult situations; maintains objectivity; keeps emotions under control; uses negotiation skills to resolve conflict.			Attendance/Punctuality – Is consistently at work and on time; ensures work responsibilities are covered when absent; arrives at meetings and appointments on time.		Dependability – Follows instructions, responds to management directions; takes responsibility for own actions; keeps commitments; commits to long hours of work when necessary to reach goals; completes task on time or notifies appropriate person with an alternate plan.		Innovation –Display original thinking and creativity; meet challenges with resourcefulness; generate suggestion for improving work; Title: Human Resource Manager
Description: 7.4.1HUMAN RESOURCE MANAGEMENTPosition Title:							Human Resource Manager	Department:								CorporateSupervisor:								CFOEmployment Status:							Full Time/ExemptSummary of Duties and Responsibilities:The Corporate Human Resource Manager is responsible for the communication and implementation of GSL Electric’s Human Resource (HR) Policies and Procedures primarily set forth in Sections 2 and 3 of GSL’s Policies and Procedures.  The Human Resource Manager is responsible for recommending updates to Sections 2 and 3 of GSL’s Policies and Procedures as policy changes are needed for Federal, State, or local jurisdictional compliance.  This position is closely coordinated with GSL’s CFO, Branch Managers, General Superintendents, Department Managers, Payroll Managers, and Benefits Manager.Recruiting:Proactively sourcing candidates for various positions within the Company through Employee-Owner referrals, job boards employment databases, social media, career fairs, responding to applicants, conducting interviews, keeping up to date on employment law and legislation while promoting company’s reputation as the ‘best place to work’.  The scope of recruiting responsibilities including the following: Develop and implement GSL Electric’s overall recruiting strategy.Prepare recruitment materials and post jobs to appropriate job boards employment databases, internal Company postings, and through social media, etc.Source and recruit candidates based on Company management requests to fill positions, using Employee-Owner notifications of open positions, posting in databases, social media, and participating in career fairs, etc.Screen candidates’ resumes and job applications.For field electricians, ensure licensing is current and active, as required by the appropriate jurisdictions (ie. DOPL site for Utah).Conduct phone screens using various reliable recruiting and selection tools/methods.Assess applicants’ relevant knowledge, hard skills, soft skills, experience, abilities, and aptitudes.Prepare candidate information with a recap of the phone screen, send to hiring managers for review.Receive feedback from hiring managers.Schedule candidate interviews with General Superintendents or other hiring managers (using Outlook calendar).Send follow-up email to candidate to confirm interview details (using GSL template) and ensure they confirm the details.Send email to referring employee with referral form attached and instructions to complete (if applicable).Provide support and current market information to hiring managers and applicants through the recruitment process.   Gather and analyze data with useful HR metrics, i.e., time it takes to fill positions, calculating and tracking employee turnover rates, and reasons for terminations (quits, lay-offs, termination for cause, etc).Maintain employee files and records.Continually research and find new ways to promote the company and source for new candidates.Coordinate with applicant and hiring managers when a job offer has been made, including the following:Make copy of IDs (or receive scanned copies - when not on site), and complete I9 process.Enter and complete case in E-Verify.Onboarding:Conduct Power Point presentation outlining policies, procedures, and benefits.Review and outline the employee manual, emphasizing important information for them to refer to when needed.Review and assist with paperwork that needs to be completed (direct deposit form, benefit forms, policy sign off forms).Collect forms and scan into appropriate folder for new hires.Ensure all updates are made and information is current on an ongoing basis pertaining to policies, procedures, and benefits. Entry Interviews:Assign and coordinate Entry Interviews to be conducted by supervisors of newly hired Employee-Owners. Follow up to ensure Entry Interviews have been completed with copies uploaded into HR Management Software. 30-Day HR Engagement Interviews:Initiate contact with new hires at about 30 days after hire to review checklist and answer any questions or concerns of new hires to help ensure they are engaging with their supervisor and with the Company.  Be sure Employee-Owners are accessing GSL’s emails and text messaging to facilitate communication within the Company.  Provide any follow-up information for the new hires as needed.  Relay any issues of concern to supervisors or higher levels of management as necessary.Annual Engagement Interviews:Conduct Annual Engagement Interviews for GSL Employee-Owners to ensure engagement with supervisors and the Company in general.  Be sure Employee-Owners are accessing GSL’s emails and text messaging to facilitate communication withing the Company.  Provide any follow-up information for the Employee-Owners as needed.  Relay any issues of concern to supervisors or higher levels of management as necessary.  Report tracking of Annual Engagement Interviews to the CFO, who will share this information with the Executive Committee.Performance Reviews:Manages the Performance Management System that GSL is utilizing to help ensure that the semi-annual or annual Performance Reviews are being conducted by the designated supervisors.  Reports the tracking of Performance Reviews to GSL’s CFO, who will share this information with the Executive Committee. Corrective Counseling:When an apparent violation of Company policy or procedures occurs, ensure the appropriate corrective counseling has been completed and documented.  Provide training to supervisors as needed on corrective counseling objectives and procedures.Terminations:When possible, conduct a Termination Interview prior to or soon after an Employee-Owner is leaving the Company or has left the Company.  Provide the information to GSL’s CFO who will share this information with the Executive Committee. Annual EEO1 Reporting:Use GSL’s internal information or GSL’s Human Resource Management software to prepare the Annual EEO1 reports and submit GSL’s EEO1 reports by the designated deadlines.As Assigned/As Necessary/On Occasion:Perform research and due diligence and follow through with compliance tasks.Maintain awareness of new, relevant Federal, State, or local jurisdictional labor laws and monitor current HR trends. Perform tasks and research as assigned or upon request by GSL Management.Qualifications:High School diploma or equivalent. Two-year to four-year degree with two years of experience, or five years of equivalent work experience.Essential Job Functions: The Human Resource Manager position requires the following essential job functions: Proficiency in Microsoft Office applications; typing at least 50 words per minute; excellent interpersonal skills with GSL Electric’s Employee-Owners  and outside vendors; ability to provide support to GSL’s Employee-Owners while communicating with GSL’s managers and executives; high level of written and verbal communications skills; prefer experience in a professional environment; strong data entry and spreadsheet experience; ability to multi-task and follow directives.  Company specific software training will be provided.Competencies, such as:Analytical Skills	    Customer Service		Delegation		Business AcumenContinuous Learning	    Communications		Leadership		Conflict ResolutionJob Knowledge	    Cooperation			Cost Consciousness	Attendance Use of Technology	    Diversity			Punctuality		Design Ability		    Teamwork		    Ethics			Dependability		Problem Solving	    Change Management	    Adaptability			Innovation		Managing Projects	    Performance Coaching   Personal Appearance	Planning/OrganizingPhysical Requirements:	Typical office working requirements allowing for significant hours devoted to computer time, email, and phone communications as required with Employee-Owners.Working Conditions:     Professional office working conditions.  Standard workdays and additional outside the office workhours may be required to meet deadlines and the needs of GSL’s Employee-Owners.Knowledge Requirements: Sufficient experience and training to be competent in following Federal, State and local jurisdictional labor laws.Skills and    Ability Requirements: Excellent communication and interpersonal skills.Problem Solving:Strong decision-making skills.Conflict resolution, ability to listen and talk with employees and offer resources if needed. Experience Requirements:Proven work experience as a Recruiter (either an in-house recruiter or a staffing agency recruiter).Familiarity with HR databases, Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS), and Candidate Management Systems (CMS) or Performance Management Systems (PMS).Hands-on experience with recruiting software, as well as Human Resource Information Systems (HRIS) or Human Resource Management Systems (HRMS).

Title: Payroll Manager
Description: 7.4.3PAYROLLPayroll ManagerThe Payroll Manager performs the following payroll processing functions:Maintains and updates employment records.  Ensures all payroll information and other employee information contained in employee files is kept confidential and secure. Updates GSL’s payroll system for changes in state and federal income tax withholding rates, state workers compensation rates, state and federal unemployment insurance rates, etc.Enters Employee/Owner information into GSL’s accounting software that is required to process payroll, including W4 and I9 information, etc.  Updates Employee/Owner data as required regarding changes in pay, tax withholdings, address changes, W4 changes, etc.  Enters such changes into the Human Resources Module in the accounting software as needed.Enters Employee/Owner’s individual information in GSL’s payroll system for GSL health insurance premiums, voluntary insurance premiums, flex spending contributions, health savings account contributions, etc., and reconciles this information periodically.Enters new employment information into payroll and provides this information to GSL’s IT and Human Resource Managers on a weekly basis.  Enters garnishments and other authorized payroll deductions into payroll and communicates such deductions to GSL’s General Ledger Manager for proper coding as needed. Enters hours into payroll after review of timecards or time sheet summaries by GSL’s General Superintendents and Business Managers.  Processes payroll on a weekly basis.Reconciles weekly payroll hours with GSL’s Job Plan hours. Uploads payroll to the bank weekly for direct deposits and issues checks as needed for Employee/Owners who resign, who are terminated for cause, or who are laid off due to a reduction of force. Tracks Employee/Owners Paid Time-Off (PTO) and reconciles PTO with Employee/Owners on an annual basis.Uploads and maintains GSL’s 401K Profit Sharing Plan’s Employee/Owner deferrals and loan payments.  Reconciles 401k Plan eligibility, deferral, and loan payments with GSL’s 401k Plan record keeper and ensures compliance for all tests related to GSL’s 401k Plan.  Prepares reports and remits payments weekly, monthly, or quarterly for payroll taxes, 401k withholdings, state withholdings, flex spending withholdings, insurance premium withholdings, and other withholdings from payroll as required. Provides verification of employment, wages and hours worked, responds to requests for unemployment claims, state or federal payroll surveys, employee census information, etc.Provides additional support and information to GSL’s CFO as needed.  Payroll AssistantDepending on the number of employees and the volume of payroll being processed, an administrative assistant may be assigned to help process payroll or to assist in completing issues related to payroll processing.
